kernelIdea: The equality axioms: reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, and closure of equality. Reflexive plus symmetric plus transitive is an equivalence relation.

kernels.l1: A thing is the same as itself. If mine matches yours, yours matches mine.
kernels.l2: Same as has three rules. Everything is the same as itself. If this matches that, then that matches this. And if this matches that and that matches the other, this matches the other.
kernels.l3: Equality obeys three rules: everything equals itself, equality can be read backwards, and equalities chain together. Any relation with all three is called an equivalence relation.
kernels.l4: Equality is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and it respects membership. Any relation with those first three properties behaves enough like equality to be called an equivalence relation.
kernels.l5: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive together define an equivalence relation. Having the same remainder is the standard example, and its classes carve the integers into disjoint families.
kernels.l6: An equivalence relation splits its set into non-overlapping classes, and every such splitting comes from one. That is the machinery behind building one number system out of another.
kernels.l7: The equality axioms are reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity and closure. The first three define an equivalence relation, whose classes divide the underlying set into non-overlapping parts — which is how each number system gets built from the one below.
kernels.l8: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive together make a relation behave like equality, which is what licenses swapping one side for the other. Such a relation splits its set into families, and those families are how every number system above the counting numbers gets built.

kernel: Axioms 1–4: reflexivity (x = x), symmetry, transitivity, and closure of equality (if x ∈ ℕ and x = y then y ∈ ℕ). Reflexive + symmetric + transitive = an equivalence relation.
objectives: Recognize them elsewhere (same age, same color, same remainder)
